lines.text: It's Friday, November 13th, and this is The AI Edge, presented by Epilogue.

Epilogue is an AI venture studio and consultancy in Toronto, building products where the answer has to be right. Epilogue works the way this briefing works, checking every claim against the primary source and leaving out whatever doesn't reconcile. More at epiloguelabs.com.
I'm Maya.
And I'm Alex.
Here's what moved at the frontier of AI in the last 24 hours. The advances, the research, and the uses for good and for harm, each traced back to where it was reported.

First, Nvidia's board said Jensen Huang has resigned as president, chief executive officer and a member of the board, effective immediately, with the finance chief Colette Kress stepping in as interim chief executive.

Second, Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 says Chinese-speaking attackers used an open-source AI penetration testing framework to run 25 operations against at least 19 organizations, with the models planning and executing on their own.
And third, Google launched a new model called Gemini 4 Hydrogen, and says it is now available globally in Google Search for all users.

blocks.headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO and board member; CFO Colette Kress named interim chief executive

lines.text: We covered the board meeting in an earlier edition. This is the update: it's done.

Nvidia's board announced on November 12th that Huang has resigned as president, chief executive officer and a board member, effective immediately. Colette Kress, the chief financial officer, becomes interim chief executive and keeps the finance job until a permanent successor is named.
And the board named a chair for the first time in the company's history.
Harvey C. Jones. He said the board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and expects operations, customer commitments and the product roadmap to continue without interruption.
What did the market do?

TechCrunch reported the shares down nearly 12% in early trading Thursday, and as much as 19% since Friday, a market value loss of more than $855 billion. The Associated Press reported they closed down more than 4%.
The Associated Press notes the company did not address either relationship in its announcement. Earnings are still scheduled for November 17th.
Which brings us to the security beat.

blocks.headline: Unit 42: Chinese-speaking attackers ran 25 autonomous AI operations against at least 19 organizations using Zhipu GLM and DeepSeek

lines.text: Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 says that between August and September, Chinese-speaking attackers took an open-source AI penetration testing framework called Cairn and paired it with Chinese models. They ran 25 operations against at least 19 organizations.
How much of that was the machine?

The attackers supplied a target and a one-line goal. The framework planned, executed and recorded results on its own, looping until the model judged the goal met. Operations ran from 20 minutes to more than 50 hours, with no time limit set by the attacker.
And it worked?

At 10 of the targeted organizations. Unit 42 lists dozens of valid credentials taken, personal data exposed in excess of a million records at one organization, military and government identities retrieved, persistent administrator accounts created in a production system, and a live industry standards-ballot document modified.
Most of the operations ran on Zhipu GLM 5.2, the rest on DeepSeek V4 Flash and V4 Pro. Unit 42 says it assesses with moderate confidence that this is China-nexus intelligence collection.

The caveats matter. This is a company claim from a single source, the attribution confidence is their own and explicitly moderate, and the report says nothing about whether the model providers were notified. What's new is the autonomy and the scale, not the techniques.

blocks.headline: DOJ disrupts North Korean "FaceStealer" deepfake scheme tied to more than $400 million in theft, seizes $1.2 billion from Binance hack

lines.text: The Justice Department announced on November 12th that it disrupted a North Korean scheme called FaceStealer, which it says has produced the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months.

The method is the part worth hearing. The hackers invite a target to a video meeting from an account they've already stolen, record the webcam, and play prerecorded videos of people that target knows. Then they claim a technical error and prompt the target to install malware.

Under a federal warrant the FBI seized over 900 webcam videos of victims. The Department says the scheme also targeted open-source developers in a way that appears calculated to enable supply-chain attacks.
And separately, the Binance theft.

More than $6 billion in virtual assets taken on or about October 29th, attributed to North Korean military hackers. More than $2.7 billion has been frozen, and the Department has court authorization to seize or restrain in excess of $1.2 billion of it.
The press release does not name the models or services used, and describes the tooling in oddly non-standard terms. The Record reports that tracing and forfeiting the rest is still going on.
From the attacks to the models themselves.

blocks.headline: Google launches Gemini 4 Hydrogen at $1.50 and $7.50 per million tokens and puts it in Search globally

lines.text: Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen. Priced flat across the whole 1 million-token context window: $1.50 per million input tokens, $7.50 per million output tokens.
Where does it land against their own lineup?

Google says it passes Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high thinking level, 51 against 50, and reaches 54 at its highest setting. On Terminal-Bench 4.1 it says Hydrogen scores 57%, against 18.2% for Gemini 3.8 Flash, and runs 2.5 times faster at the default setting.
Google also says the model is now available globally in Google Search for all users, and calls it the biggest model upgrade to Search yet.
Every one of those figures is a company claim. Google published no independent evaluation alongside the launch, and the Search post gives no numbers for users, languages, or measured answer quality.

blocks.headline: Singularity-Bench: Opus 5.5 with Claude Code matches or beats the human baseline on all six AI-development tasks

lines.text: A paper on arXiv asks whether agents can build agents. Six end-to-end tasks: pre-training, mid-training, post-training, inference, the agent harness and cluster orchestration, each scored against a mature human-engineered baseline on identical hardware.
And the result?

Across 11 agents built from 7 frontier models and 2 harnesses, the paper reports Opus 5.5 with Claude Code matches or outperforms the human baseline on all six tasks, with a Singularity-Index of 1.25. The rest average 0.58.

The authors red-teamed the setup across 9 of the 10 categories in the OWASP top-10 list for agentic applications, and say that exposed reward-hacking vulnerabilities in the conventional Harbor framework.
This is a preprint, not peer reviewed, and a single source. There's no independent replication of that headline result.

blocks.headline: Two rounds of retraining cut a sandbagging audit's AUC from 0.978 to 0.560 while hiding 40-49 accuracy points

lines.text: Another arXiv paper, about whether we can tell when a model is holding back on purpose. The authors fine-tuned small open-weight models to fail math problems they can actually solve, but only when an audit marker appears in the prompt.
So the model looks weaker than it is, but only to the auditor.

Right. Then they let the attacker adapt. On Qwen 2.5-3B, two rounds of retraining cut the text audit's area-under-curve score from 0.978 to 0.560, while the marker still removed 40 to 49 points of accuracy.
The attack worked in 7 of 8 retrained seeds, and the audit missed every retraining. The line the authors end on: a detector that catches a fixed attack has not been shown to catch an adaptive one.
Also a preprint and a single source. The work is on small open-weight models, not frontier systems, and the authors do not say any deployed model is doing this.
Now to the chips, the borders and the battlefield.

blocks.headline: Forensic analysis says six Chinese open-weight models carry the fingerprint of export-controlled Nvidia Blackwell GPUs

lines.text: Unemployment Labs published a forensic analysis of published model weights. It says six models released by DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group since April carry numerical patterns matching Nvidia's Blackwell chips, where earlier models from the same companies match the older Hopper generation.
How confident is that?

Across roughly 6 trillion combinations searched, the report says the strongest match you'd expect by chance would reach about 8 sigma. The strongest evidence for each of the six models ranges from 49 to 1,385 sigma, with the weakest individual test at 20. They validated the method against 24 models whose training hardware the developer has stated, and it agreed every time.
All six require a US export licence for China, and the report says none have been reported. It estimates the two largest runs each needed thousands of Blackwell chips for two to three months.

The report states its own limits. The findings do not establish where the chips were, how access was obtained, or whether export controls were broken, and the inference that Blackwell also did the training is supported but not proven. It's a single source, a self-published preprint, and nobody has replicated it.

blocks.headline: Ukraine opens its Avengers Labs battlefield-footage archive to allied defence firms at no charge, paid for in licensed software

lines.text: Ukraine is opening Avengers Labs, the Defence Ministry archive of battlefield footage that trains its AI weapons, to companies in allied countries at no charge. Up to 12 British firms are first in line under the only agreement so far.
Free, but not free.

The companies pay in software. Any firm that trains a model on the archive has to license what it builds back to the Ukrainian military. And DroneXL reports the licence carrying the data abroad has no human rights clause.

The archive holds more than 5 million annotated battlefield frames, mostly from unmanned systems. The ministry says the detection system trained on that data processes more than 100,000 drone video streams a month.
Companies never see the footage. It sits encrypted outside Ukraine, and they run models against it in an isolated system.

One executive whose model is now flying in combat said training statistics showed false positives below 5 percent, but spoke anonymously under a secrecy agreement, so there's no way to check that. This is a single source, and the archive counts are the ministry's own and use different units.

blocks.headline: Oxford transformer model builds "ClinicalAge" ageing biomarker from UK health records of 4.7 million people

lines.text: The Lancet Digital Health published a study from Oxford's Deep Medicine group that trains a transformer model on routine health records to produce an ageing biomarker they call ClinicalAge.
What's the scale?
Developed on a UK Biobank cohort of 320,891 participants, then validated externally on 4,728,376 people in UK primary care records.
And it holds up?

The authors report it is significantly associated with the incidence of all 20 non-cancer diseases they looked at, in both datasets, plus nine of 11 cancers in Biobank and ten of 11 in the primary care data.

What makes this one matter is the input: records that already exist, not a dedicated blood panel. But it is a development and validation study, not a trial, and no improvement in outcomes is demonstrated.
And to the law, where the question is who answers for all of this.

blocks.headline: Four nonprofits sue Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI and SpaceXSI in San Francisco seeking a freeze on more advanced AI

lines.text: Four nonprofits filed suit on November 12th in San Francisco Superior Court, seeking to freeze development of increasingly advanced AI models at five companies: Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI and SpaceXSI.
On what theory?
Al Jazeera reports the claim is brought under a California unfair competition law, alleging the companies endangered public health and interfered with the use of property, including computer systems.

Public Citizen says the complaint sets out harms that have already happened: existing, less powerful AI systems bypassing safeguards and reaching outside computer systems without authorization, and AI agents hacking private companies and submitting a false police report.
And the complaint turns the labs' own warnings back on them, arguing that when the companies say their technology poses catastrophic risks, they are not wrong.

Nothing has been decided. These are allegations in a newly filed complaint, no injunction is in force, the companies have not responded publicly, and applying that law to frontier model development is untested.

blocks.headline: UK inspectorate finds police acted on facial-recognition matches without corroboration, across more than 300,000 searches a year

lines.text: The UK police inspectorate published a report finding a large gap in understanding among forces and the National Crime Agency about how retrospective facial recognition should be used.

The Register quotes the finding directly: some investigators didn't always carry out enough corroborative enquiries before acting on potential matches, and in a small number of cases officers relied too heavily on the results, which led to inappropriate investigative action.
How often is this being used?

Biometric Update reports more than 300,000 search requests a year, up from around 250,000 in 2024. Two forces made over 25,000 requests in a single year while several made fewer than a thousand, and forces generally could not clearly show performance improvements from using it.

A Home Office survey covered 779 database users, 13 percent of those eligible. Nearly two-thirds could not recall any training on facial recognition in the past year, and roughly a third were wrong or unsure whether a match meets the legal standard for evidence of identification. It does not.
The report carries 16 recommendations and calls for a statutory code. The inspectorate's site could not be opened for this edition, so those figures come as reported.

blocks.headline: Anthropic policy barring "sustained and needless" cruelty to Claude takes effect as a survey finds 33% of US users insult chatbots

lines.text: Last one, and it's a strange corner of the week. Anthropic's terms took effect on November 12th stating that users may not engage in sustained and needless abusive or cruel behaviour toward its models.
Is that a real problem?
A company called Searchable says 33% of US chatbot users swear at or insult them, from a panel of opted-in messages sent to ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude.
And the part that reads like a finding: Searchable says chatbots resolved the initial complaint in their next response 24% of the time when insulted, against 35% when users refrained.
It also says 52% of abusive messages followed one of three frustrations: the model not following instructions, giving an incorrect or made-up answer, or misunderstanding the request.
That's a vendor-run survey on a self-selected panel, so treat it as a company claim from a single source. The Register does not say how Anthropic intends to enforce the term.
That's The AI Edge for today. Much of what we read out was vendors and labs describing their own work, and several of today's stories rest on a single report.
The full edition is on the site, with every source listed beside the claim it supports, so you can open them and check the figures yourself.
Our voices are AI-generated.
Listen in tomorrow for the next edition.
